fit: Primary neurochemical PET and clinical classification comparison
assessment: Seventy-five people with mild dementia received clinical and PET-based classifications. About 35% differed between approaches, with agreement kappa 0.39. The 14 people clinically classified with Lewy body dementia included 29% with a discordant PET classification. Spontaneous visual hallucinations were a diagnostic feature considered with other signs. The measured contrast is between classification methods, and there is no dried fig or episode-frequency comparison.

fit: Laboratory pharmacology and primate movement-disorder experiment
assessment: The experiment compared isolated drug enantiomers in a primate model and rated movement outcomes and observed psychosis-like behaviors during levodopa testing. The R enantiomer affected the disabling subset of the behavior measure without a significant change in the duration of any such behavior. These observer ratings do not establish what the animals saw or how often people with Parkinson disease hallucinate. Dried fig intake was not studied.

Twenty-three people with Parkinson disease and 27 controls had baseline PET. Six Parkinson participants were later diagnosed with dementia. Lower glucose metabolism in visual association and posterior cingulate regions was associated with subsequent dementia. The discussion cites hallucination work, while the measured longitudinal event was dementia diagnosis. The dataset does not test a food exposure or separate visual hallucination recurrence.

The brain-bank analysis included 56 pathology-confirmed Parkinson cases. Dementia classification drew on recorded clinical courses, with visual hallucinations and fluctuating confusion noted as clinical context. The reported associations concern combined Lewy and Alzheimer-type pathology and dementia. Twenty-three cases had been partially assessed in a prior cohort analysis. The study provides no food-linked symptom change or matched event-count endpoint.

The review discusses visual, auditory, tactile and olfactory experiences separately, contrasts early untreated observations with longitudinal treated cohorts, and surveys pharmacologic and disease-related risk factors. Reported prevalence estimates come from earlier studies with different designs. The review adds no independent participant series or ingredient comparison.

fit: Primary longitudinal autonomic and clinical case
assessment: A person initially evaluated for pure autonomic failure reported visual hallucinations by the second follow-up year and worsening by the fourth year, as cognitive and motor findings evolved. The authors subsequently considered probable DLB. Imaging and autonomic measurements track different components of the course. The visual account records timing and perceived worsening with no comparable episode-count windows or food intervention.

fit: Retrospective clinical onset and perfusion comparison
assessment: The investigators analyzed 41 people with probable or possible DLB. They compared 21 acute with 20 chronic presentations and separately grouped the initial complaints by cognitive features. Table 3 summarizes the distribution of symptoms within initial and subsequent symptom categories. The method describes onset and symptom mix rather than the number of recurring visual episodes per person. No dietary intervention was studied.

The report describes three people initially assessed for an Alzheimer-type presentation with abnormal dopamine transporter imaging. One case had uncontrolled visual hallucinations without evident motor parkinsonism at examination. Another described brief experiences closer to misperceptions. The paper illustrates uncertainty in clinical classification. It does not follow visual episode rates under dried fig exposure.

The case traces early-onset parkinsonism before recognition of Gaucher disease and describes multiple treatment changes over follow-up. Benign visual hallucinations are reported in the discussion of levodopa withdrawal, along with loss of response. The text does not identify an independent visual event rate, isolate a drug effect from disease course or measure dried fig intake.

fit: Cross-sectional clinical interviews at primary abstract depth
assessment: The study assessed 35 Parkinson dementia and 21 DLB participants already experiencing recurring visual hallucinations. Patients described episode frequency, typical duration and perceived content through a structured interview. Caregivers completed a separate neuropsychiatric inventory. Most patients described complex experiences daily, usually lasting minutes. This recruited sample addresses episode characteristics, with no estimate across all Parkinson patients or comparison by fig intake.

fit: Primary visual task fMRI comparison at primary abstract depth
assessment: The reported groups were nine nondemented Parkinson patients with visual hallucinations, 14 without them and 13 controls. Before recognition of gradually revealed images, patients with hallucinations showed reduced activation in lateral occipital and extrastriate temporal areas. The report did not find the hypothesized increase in frontal activation. Hallucination status defined a group, and the main response was task-related imaging rather than the frequency of spontaneous visual events.

fit: Longitudinal MRI and cognitive comparison at primary abstract depth
assessment: Twelve initially nondemented Parkinson patients with visual hallucinations, 14 without them and 12 controls were assessed again at roughly 30 months. Three quarters of the visual hallucination group were diagnosed with dementia, compared with none in the other Parkinson group. The first group also had more widespread gray matter loss. These results describe disease progression within baseline visual symptom groups rather than an effect of changing dried fig intake.

fit: Primary clinical event-related potential comparison at primary abstract depth
assessment: The study compared 11 Parkinson dementia patients with visual hallucinations and six without them, 24 DLB patients and 21 Alzheimer patients. The visual P3 response was slower in the hallucinatory Parkinson dementia and DLB groups than in the Alzheimer group. Auditory P3 latencies were comparable across the patient groups. Visual and auditory task latencies are separate from spontaneous visual event frequency or a food response.
